summary.text: The geologic time scale divides Earth's history, a span of about 4.54 billion years, into standard intervals.
It puts rock layers in relative order using principles such as the law of superposition, then uses methods like radiometric dating to fix the ages of the boundaries between them.
Its official units are set by the International Commission on Stratigraphy, which defines many boundaries at a precise point in a specific rock section, nicknamed a golden spike.

facts.label: Span covered
facts.value: About 4.54 billion years of Earth history

items.prompt: A road cut exposes flat, undisturbed layers of sediment. Which layer was laid down first?

options.label: The thickest layer
The layer at the top
The layer in the middle
The layer at the bottom

items.explain: By the law of superposition, in undeformed sequences the oldest strata lie at the bottom and newer material stacks on top.

items.prompt: A band of volcanic rock slices straight through three layers of sandstone. What can a geologist conclude?

options.label: The volcanic band is younger than the sandstone
The volcanic band is older than the sandstone
The sandstone formed after the volcanic band
They must have formed at the same moment

items.explain: By the principle of cross-cutting relationships, a rock that cuts across another must be younger than the rock it cuts.

items.prompt: A geologist finds chunks of one kind of rock embedded inside a second kind of rock. Which rock is older?

options.label: The surrounding rock, since it holds the chunks
The rock the chunks are made of
Neither, since embedding resets both ages
Whichever rock is harder

items.explain: By the law of included fragments, embedded fragments must have formed first and were caught up as the second rock formed.

items.prompt: Two cliffs hundreds of kilometres apart show the same distinctive sets of fossils, stacked in the same order. What does this let geologists do?

options.label: Prove the two cliffs were once a single cliff
Give each layer an exact age in years
Match layers of the same age between the cliffs
Show the fossils moved between the cliffs later

items.explain: Faunal succession says fossil sets follow each other in a reliable order, which allows strata to be correlated even when they are not continuous.

items.prompt: Rocks around the world record the moment the Cretaceous gave way to the Paleogene. What marks that boundary?

options.label: A layer of ice-scraped gravel from a glaciation
An iridium anomaly left by the Chicxulub asteroid impact
A sudden shift in Earth's magnetic field direction
The first fossils of animals with shells

items.explain: The iridium anomaly from the Chicxulub impact marks the lower boundary of the Paleogene, and strata containing it are found worldwide.

items.prompt: Improved dating shifts the age of the start of the Cambrian Period by over two million years. What happens to the rock layer that defines that boundary?

options.label: It stays the same; only the age assigned to it changes
It moves to a deeper layer in the rock record
It moves to a higher layer in the rock record
It is dropped and a new boundary is chosen elsewhere

items.explain: When the Cambrian's base was revised from 541 Ma to 538.8 Ma, its rock definition at the GSSP did not change; only the absolute age was refined.

beats.title: Reading Earth's Stacked Pages
beats.hook: A cliff face is a stack of history, and a handful of simple rules tell you which layer came first.

beats.prompt: You find pebbles of limestone embedded inside a layer of sandstone. What does that tell you about the two rocks?
beats.explain: By the law of included fragments, pieces of one rock embedded in a second rock must have formed first and were included as the second rock formed.

choices.label: The sandstone formed first, then grew the limestone inside it
choices.feedback: This reverses the order: the pebbles had to exist before the rock around them formed.

choices.label: Their order cannot be told without fossils
choices.feedback: No fossils are needed here; the embedded pieces alone reveal which rock came first.

choices.label: The limestone formed first, then got caught up in the sandstone
Both rocks formed at exactly the same time
choices.feedback: Tempting because they sit together, but the pebbles were already solid rock when the sandstone formed around them.

beats.prompt: Match each principle to what it says.

right.label: Oldest layers lie at the bottom
A rock that cuts another is younger
Fossil sets follow a reliable order
Sediments are first laid down flat

beats.explain: Each principle lets geologists work out which rocks are older or younger without knowing their exact ages.

beats.prompt: Sort each into rock units (chronostratigraphic) or time units (geochronologic).
beats.explain: A system is the body of rock laid down during an interval; the matching period is the interval of time itself.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning is wrong; which?

steps.text: The base of the Cambrian Period was once dated at 541 Ma.
In 2022, better dating revised that age to 538.8 Ma.
So the golden spike at the base of the Cambrian had to be moved to a different rock layer.
The boundary between the Ediacaran and Cambrian systems is still defined at the same point in the rock.

beats.explain: Improved dating changes the age of a time unit, but the rock definition of the boundary (its GSSP) stays where it is; only the absolute age is refined.

beats.idea: Rules about how rock layers stack and cut each other give their relative order, and dating methods then fix the ages of the boundaries.
